_note: Conversation scenes. Each plays after the expedition named in 'after', when every companion in 'cast' is in the party; otherwise the party goes straight to town. Lines are {"say": companion id or name, "text"} or {"narrate"}. A choice's 'next' names another node of the same scene; no 'next' returns to town. 'sameAs' copies another node's lines. Choices change companion approval only, never XP or loot.

night.title: The Night after the Bridge
night.objective: Sit with your companions after the bridge.

lines.narrate: The refugee camp below Ashford has gone quiet. Someone has lent your party a cooking pot, and Maren has used it. She hands you the first bowl.

lines.text: What is this.
Stew.
It's grey, Maren.
It has nourishment. Colours are a luxury of the well-provisioned.

lines.narrate: Nessa tips her bowl toward the dog that has followed the carts all the way from the bridge. The dog sniffs it, considers, and lies down facing the other way.

lines.text: Biscuit agrees with me.
You named the dog.
He named himself. I just guessed right.

lines.narrate: Orin hasn't touched his bowl. He is scrubbing the lid of the borrowed pot, slowly and carefully, and the lid is already clean.

lines.text: Orin. That's the third time you've cleaned that.
Fourth. You weren't watching for the first one.

lines.narrate: The child from the last cart is asleep against a wheel twenty paces away, still wearing the blanket Orin gave her.

lines.text: She asked me if soldiers always leave first. On the bridge. I didn't have an answer.

choices.label: “You didn't leave. That's your answer.”

lines.narrate: Orin is quiet for a long moment. Then he sets down the lid and picks up his bowl.

lines.text: Nice thing to say. Doesn't make it true for her.
It's true enough for tonight.

choices.label: “Tell her the truth tomorrow. All of it.”

lines.narrate: Maren nods before Orin does.

lines.text: All of it is a long story.
Then start with the short part.

choices.label: “Sometimes they do.”

lines.narrate: Nobody speaks. Maren looks at you as if you had kicked something. Then Orin nods, once, as if you have finally said something true.

lines.text: Yes. Sometimes they do.
That is not what a frightened child needs to hear.
It's what I needed to hear.

choices.label: Say nothing and sit beside him

lines.narrate: You sit. The fire pops. After a while Nessa gets up without a word and slides her bowl across to Orin. Biscuit follows the bowl.

lines.text: He's yours now. The dog, not the stew. Well. Both.

lines.narrate: Later, when the fire is low, Orin eats the stew. All of it. Maren watches him do it and says nothing.

lines.text: It's terrible.
It's nourishing.

choices.label: Get some sleep
Get some sleep

breakfast.title: Morning in the Camp
breakfast.objective: See what Orin does with the truth.

lines.narrate: Morning comes grey and cold. The child from the last cart is called Wenna, it turns out, and she finds Orin before he can find her.

lines.text: You're the one who gave me the blanket.
I am.
Do I have to give it back?
No.

lines.narrate: She nods, satisfied, and waits. Orin crouches so his eyes are level with hers. It takes him a long time to get all the way down.

lines.text: You asked me if soldiers always leave first. Sometimes they do. I did, once. A long time ago, at a place a lot like that bridge.
Did the people get across?
Not all of them.

lines.narrate: Wenna considers this with great seriousness.

lines.text: You didn't leave this time.
No.
Then you're getting better at it.

lines.narrate: She goes back to her mother with the blanket trailing in the mud. Orin stays crouched there until Maren offers him a hand up, and for once he takes it.

lines.text: That was badly done.
I know.
It was also the truest thing I have heard you say in a year.

choices.label: Head back into Ashford

chairs-camp.location: The wall walk at Highpass, after the council

wall.title: Sergeant at Arms
wall.objective: Sit with your companions before Fenmere.

lines.narrate: Long after midnight the wall walk is empty except for your party. Highpass's ward is still humming, softly, like a kettle that has nearly boiled. Somewhere below, three hundred refugees are asleep in tents that are still there.
Orin has the confiscated knives laid out on the parapet in a row, labelled. He is writing a list.

lines.text: You're giving them back.
In the morning. With the list.
Nobody asked you to make a list.
Sorrel said keep order.
She didn't mean the knives, Orin.
I know what she meant. The knives I could do something about.

lines.narrate: Nessa has a letter in her lap she hasn't been writing. She has been holding the pen for some time.

lines.text: Who's that one to?
Nobody. Wren. Nobody. It's not finished.
None of them are ever finished.
That's how you know they're good.

choices.label: “Send it, Nessa. This one, at least.”

lines.text: And say what? 'Dear Wren, the council argued about chairs, there's a goat'?
She'd want to know about the goat.

lines.narrate: Nessa looks at him as if he has said something unexpectedly wise, and then folds the letter and puts it in her pocket, the one for later. Not the other one.

choices.label: “What did you all make of Provost Marrow?”

lines.text: She doesn't lie. I listened all day. She doesn't even shade the truth, which is rarer.
Corvane didn't lie either.
No. That's what worries me.
I liked her. She did the chairs in five minutes.
So would I, if I'd drawn the room.

lines.narrate: Below, the camp's last fire goes out. Orin finishes his list, reads it through once, and adds the bread knife at the bottom, with a note: returned.

choices.label: Get some sleep before Fenmere

fenmere-bakery.location: Fenmere, the edge of the white field

shop.title: The Baker's Ward
shop.objective: Help the last of the lower village close up.

lines.narrate: On the morning you are due to leave, Ilka comes to find you. There is one house at the very edge of the white field, half in and half out of the mist, where the frost has stopped at the doorstep. It is the bakery. The baker, Tam Orrey, went back for his starter dough on the first night, and did not come back up.
The door opens on a warm room. The ovens are lit. There are loaves on the racks, golden and perfect, and when you touch one it isn't there. In the back, the oven fire turns to look at you.

lines.text: We open at six.
It's his ward. Bakers keep a little one in the oven, to keep the bread from going mouldy and the shop from going cold. It's been holding the Gloam back off this one shop for four days.
Tam's gone for flour. We open at six. You can wait.
It doesn't know.
He's often late. He talks. Customers like it. We open at six.

choices.label: Tell the ward, gently, that Tam is not coming back

lines.narrate: The fire listens. It is a long time before it says anything.

lines.text: He went for the starter. It was his grandmother's. I told him not to.
Wards don't say no to their keepers. You couldn't have stopped him.
I could have kept the door shut.

lines.narrate: Maren sits down on a flour sack and stays with it, the way she stays with people. In the end the fire says it would like to close up properly, and asks you to turn the sign on the door. You turn it. CLOSED. The frost comes in over the doorstep very slowly, as if it has been asked to wipe its feet.

choices.label: Fetch Brannagh: she knew Tam

lines.narrate: Brannagh comes down with the goat. She looks at the warm shop and the loaves that aren't there.

lines.text: Ward. It's Brannagh. Tam's dead. You knew that, I expect.
...yes.
Then stop baking. You're making the whole village hungry and there's nothing to eat.

lines.narrate: The fire makes a sound which in a person would be a laugh, and then something else. Brannagh turns the sign herself. On the way out she takes one of the loaves that isn't there, and holds it all the way up the hill.

choices.label: Let it keep the shop until six, as it wants

lines.narrate: You wait. Nobody says anything. At six the ward opens the door, and the frost takes the doorstep, and the counter, and the oven, very quietly, and the warm room goes white. It does not seem to mind. It is open.

lines.text: That was kind. I'm not sure it was right.

after.title: Leaving Fenmere
after.objective: Take the road west to Briarwatch.

lines.narrate: On the road west, Maren takes out her list of lost keepers. She looks at it for a while. Then she writes a new name at the bottom, in small careful letters: Tam Orrey, baker, Fenmere. And beside it, already: closed up.

choices.label: Go home to Briarwatch

southroad-camp.location: The beacon station at Kell's Bridge

fire.title: Old Company
fire.objective: Sit up with Orin and Hal.

lines.narrate: Late, with the soldiers asleep in the station, Orin and Hal sit by the cabbage-patch fire. They are not talking. You sit down with them anyway, and after a while they forget you are there.

lines.text: You didn't answer my letter.
You asked me to sign on with you. Central Command. Steady pay.
I did.
I couldn't say yes. And I couldn't write that I'd think about it, because I wasn't going to. So I didn't write.
You could have written that it was a bad idea.
It was a bad idea.
I know that now. Took me a summer and a cabbage patch.

lines.narrate: Hal laughs, a short tired bark of a laugh, and puts another stick on the fire. Orin doesn't laugh. He is looking at the beacon frame on top of the tower, where the echo-stones used to hang.

lines.text: Forty of you out here. Nobody came. I should have come.

choices.label: “Say the rest of it, Orin.”

lines.text: I left you out here. Not on purpose. That's no excuse.
Stoneward. You came. Late, with a council and a goat-woman's money. But you came.
Stoneward. You came. Late, with a council and a lamp-seller's loan. But you came.
Stoneward. You came. Late, and with your friend's own fee in the first cart, I hear. But you came.

lines.narrate: Hal goes off to check on the sentries, who don't need checking on. Orin stays by the fire and, for the first time since Briarwatch, looks like a man who is sitting down rather than waiting to stand up.

choices.label: Leave them to it

lines.narrate: You get up and go. Behind you, after a while, you hear them start talking: about the Ashford span, about people you never met, about a quartermaster in the Second Company who used to steal everyone's boots. Then, eventually, laughing.

harbour-camp.location: The inn on the Merrowgate quays, after midnight

invoice.title: Settling Up
invoice.objective: Sit with the party after the sale.

lines.narrate: Long after midnight, Iona finds your party in the inn's back room. She has changed her coat, and her wrists are bandaged, and she has her invoice book.

lines.text: I've been thinking about my invoice.
We were going to pay it.
No, you weren't, and I didn't expect you to. That's not the point. The point is, I've added a line.

lines.narrate: She tears out the page and puts it on the table. Under the beer and the cart, in the same neat hand, there is a new entry.

lines.text: 'To retrieval of the quartermaster from the lantern-works, at the hero's expense: one evening. Credit.' And then the total.
We're square, as of tonight. I don't do that often. Don't tell Ashford.
What are you going to do about Elske's proposal?
Vote for it, probably. I was tied to a chair for a day because five towns couldn't decide who held the purse. Somebody should be able to say 'stop' faster than that.

lines.narrate: She goes. Orin looks at the invoice for a while, then folds it and puts it in his pack.

choices.label: “You're keeping that?”

lines.text: It's the only thank-you letter I've ever had that adds up.
Orin Stoneward. That was very nearly a joke.
It was a joke.

choices.label: “What did you make of Elske tonight?”

lines.text: She asked for power in front of the whole city and told them how to take it away from her. I've never seen anyone do that.
Corvane would have liked to have been asked, too. Once.
That's not fair.
No. It's what I'm afraid of. Fair's got nothing to do with it.

keeper-cards.location: The Sallows hospice, the next evening

cards.title: Bring Cards
cards.objective: Play a hand at the hospice.

lines.narrate: The next evening, the lamps in the Sallows are lit along the whole street, and the hospice door is open, because it can be.
The next evening, six new lamps are lit along the hospice street. Past the corner, the rest of the Sallows is as dark as it was. The hospice door is open, because it can be.
Anwen has set up a card table in the long room. The patients who are well enough have pulled their beds round to watch.

lines.text: Three-handed Lowmere. Vale knows the rules. You'll pick them up. Or you won't, and that's also fine, because we're playing for buttons.

lines.narrate: It takes about four hands to understand that Maren and Anwen are cheating. It takes another four to understand they are cheating in exactly the same way, and that each of them knows it, and that the game they are actually playing is about who will be the first to say so.
A patient in the end bed, who used to deal cards on the ferries, has worked it out too. He catches your eye and very slowly shakes his head: don't.
The patients are crying with laughter. An old fisherman who has not been able to remember his wife's name for a month says it, out loud, by accident, and stops laughing, and then starts again.

lines.text: You taught me that one.
I taught you all of them, Vale. That's why you're losing.

choices.label: Call it: “You're both cheating.”

lines.narrate: Both of them turn on you at once, with exactly the same expression of injured innocence. The fisherman falls off his bed.

lines.text: Vale, your friend has no manners.
None. It's one of the things I like about them.

choices.label: Lose gracefully and keep watching

lines.narrate: You lose every button you have. It is the best evening anyone in the long room has had in a year.
Afterwards, on the tide steps, Maren takes out her list. Every name has something written beside it now, except one. She looks at Anwen's name for a long time with the pencil in her hand.

lines.text: I don't know what to write. Found isn't right. She was never lost. She was busy.

choices.label: “Write that she chose.”

lines.narrate: Maren writes it. Chose. Then she folds the list, very carefully, and for the first time since you have known her she does not put it back in her pocket. She drops it into the harbour and watches it go.

lines.text: Six years. That's enough lists.

choices.label: “Leave it blank. It's not finished.”

lines.narrate: Maren nods slowly and puts the list back in her pocket, with the one empty space.

lines.text: No. You're right. It isn't.

night.title: After Hollin's Reach
night.objective: Sit with your companions after the burned town.

lines.narrate: Nobody can sleep. The inn at Cinder Fold is warm all through, because the whole mountain is warm, and somehow that makes it worse.

Nobody has made supper. Maren sits with her hands in her lap, which you have never seen her do; there is always something in them. Orin is at the window, looking at the forge-glow on the mountain, which is the wrong colour to be a fire and still looks like one.

lines.text: Eleven years she's carried that room. On her own.
Not on her own. She built a machine to carry it for her.
In the memory. When you stood up. Were you sure?
In the memory. When you went up that tower into the fire. Were you sure?
In the memory. When it all went to fire and you kept going anyway. Were you sure?

choices.label: “Yes.”

lines.text: Good. Somebody should be, at the vote. I'm not.

choices.label: “No. I just knew how it ended.”

lines.text: That's what Elske wants. Someone who knows how it ends.
Nobody does. That's the whole trouble.

cinderfold-camp.location: The peak stairs above Cinder Fold

stairs.title: The Peak Stairs
stairs.objective: Climb to the forge-signal with Nessa and Wren.

lines.narrate: The forge-signal is a beacon on the peak, four hundred steps above the town. Wren insists on climbing them, for the last time, she says, with her stick and her bad leg and Nessa's arm, which she pretends she is not leaning on.

lines.text: Slow down.
I am going slow.
You're going slow for you. Go slow for me.

lines.narrate: Halfway up Wren stops to breathe, and Nessa stops with her, and they stand side by side looking down at the town. They have exactly the same way of standing. Both of them notice at the same moment, and both of them shift their weight to the other foot to stop doing it, and then they've done that the same way too.

lines.text: Oh, for pity's sake.
That's what you sound like when you're cross.
That's what you sound like when you're cross, girl. I had it first.

lines.narrate: At the top, Wren shows Nessa how the beacon is laid, and how it is lit, and where the oil is kept, and which of the stairs are loose. She does not say why. Nessa does not ask.

choices.label: Hand Nessa the taper

lines.narrate: Nessa lights the beacon. It goes up all at once, a column of orange, and every chimney in Cinder Fold below answers it with a puff of smoke, as if the town were breathing out.

lines.text: Not bad. Bit fast.
It's meant to be fast.
I know. I've just never seen it from this side.

choices.label: Let Wren light it, one last time

lines.narrate: Wren lights the beacon, slowly, with great care, the way she has done it every night for a year. Nessa watches her hands the whole time, the way you watch someone do a thing you are about to have to do yourself.

lines.text: You're slow.
I'm thorough. You'll get there.

vote-camp.location: Dera's forge, the night after the vote

forge.title: Midwinter at the Forge
forge.objective: Sit with your companions after the vote.

lines.narrate: Dera's forge, after midnight. Dera has gone to bed, leaving the fire banked and a jug on the anvil with a note: DON'T TOUCH THE TONGS.
Brannagh's goat is asleep by the fire in its blanket. Nobody knows where Brannagh is. Nobody is going to wake the goat to ask.

lines.text: Did we do the right thing?
We did a thing. Ask me in a year.
We did a thing. Ask me when the mist comes back.
That's not an answer.
It's the only honest one I've got.

choices.label: “It was the right thing.”

lines.text: You sound very sure.
Somebody should be. It isn't going to be me.

choices.label: “I don't know. I don't think anyone does.”

lines.text: No. I think that might be the right answer, actually.

lines.narrate: Maren reaches over and, very carefully, without touching the tongs, takes the jug.

oath-epilogue.location: Cinder Fold, then home to Briarwatch

oath.title: The Second Oath
oath.objective: Swear who your oath answers to.

lines.narrate: Before the council rises, Aveline asks you to swear it, for the record: who does the hero of the free wards answer to? There is no right answer in the charter. There is no page for it. She dips her pen and waits.
You remember the oath you swore on the road at level ten, to the people who cannot hold the road themselves.
You remember the oath you swore on the road at level ten, to the ones who walk it with you.
You remember the oath you swore on the road at level ten, to every town on the road, even the ones that cannot agree.

choices.label: “To the council. It can recall me, like anyone.”

lines.narrate: Aveline writes it down. Then, after a moment, she adds a line, and reads it out: 'Recallable by two-thirds.' The council votes on it. It is the fastest vote anyone has ever seen.

lines.text: Noted. We can be quick when we feel like it.

choices.label: “To Briarwatch. It took me in.”

lines.narrate: Aveline stops writing, and looks at you, and for a moment the tiredness goes out of her face entirely.

lines.text: Briarwatch will hold you to it. Briarwatch holds everyone to everything. Ask Tovin.

choices.label: “To the people I walk with.”

lines.narrate: Aveline writes down three names, and then, after a glance at the fire, a fourth: Biscuit.
Aveline writes down their names, one after another, with great care.

lines.text: We'll hold you to it.
Constantly.

choices.label: “To no one. To what's right, as best I can see it.”

lines.narrate: Aveline writes it down without a word. Elske, across the circle, closes her eyes for a moment.

lines.text: That's what I said, at your age. Be better at it than I was.

lines.narrate: In the spring, your party comes home to Briarwatch, and Dera has your gear on the bench before you have finished saying hello.

lines.text: You broke it. Again. What was it this time?
A council.
That'll do it.

lines.narrate: Tovin rings the hours. Pim rings them with him, exactly on time, every time, and has been told to breathe so often that he now does it without being asked. Aveline sleeps, people say, for a week.
Brannagh has her fence. The goat ignores it entirely.

Maren's list is gone; she let it go in Merrowgate harbour. She has started a new one. It is the names of the people in the Sallows long room, and beside each one is something true about them. The last name on it is Elske Marrow's. Beside it Maren has written: comes every week, and reads to them.

Maren still has her list, with one empty space on it. She has stopped looking at it every night. She is waiting, she says, for the right word to turn up. Below the space, in newer ink, there is one more name: Elske Marrow. Beside it she has written nothing yet, either. When you ask, she says Elske isn't finished.
Orin has the quartermaster's invoice in his pack. Sometimes, when he thinks nobody is looking, he reads it.

choices.label: Ask Nessa what she has decided about Wren's post

lines.narrate: Nessa has been carrying a letter since Cinder Fold. She takes it out now, and for once she does not put it back in the pocket for later.

lines.text: It's to Wren. It says yes. Well. It says 'yes, but not yet, I've got a council to keep an eye on, and you're not dead, so you can manage another winter.' It's a long yes.
I'm going to send it. Actually send it. Will you walk to the carters with me?

lines.narrate: You walk to the carters with her. She hands it over herself, and watches the cart all the way out of sight, and then turns round and asks what's for supper.

choices.label: Sit by Dera's fire a while

end.title: Briarwatch
end.objective: Book Two is complete. Choose your 2nd job when you reach level 20.

lines.narrate: The bell sounds once across the wet roofs of Briarwatch, as it did at the end of the first story: not an alarm. An answer. And from far off, too faint to be sure of, other bells answer it, each in its own voice.
This is the end of the written story of Briarwatch. The roads go on.
This is the end of Book Two, The Council of Small Voices. The roads go on, and somewhere down them, the old bells are waiting.

choices.label: Go out into Briarwatch

letter-camp.location: Dera's forge, the night after the cart

forge.title: What They Know of the Commandery
forge.objective: Sit with your companions by the forge.

lines.narrate: Roke is asleep in Dera's back room. The forge fire is banked. Corvane's letter lies on the anvil, where nobody has to look at it unless they want to.

lines.text: Has anyone actually been there? The Commandery. Not the beacon. There.
Once. When I was a novice. The shrine at Upper Morrow had a keeper who had been taken for service, and I was sent to ask after her. They gave me tea and a receipt.
Upper Morrow is on his list.

lines.narrate: Nessa looks at the letter, and then away from it.

lines.text: I know the echo-stones. From the signal tower. Wren used to read their pulses off the mirror, every hour on the hour, Central Command's relays all down the Iron Road. She said you could tell when an officer was in a bad mood by the rhythm.
She said you couldn't tell anything else. That was the point of them. Everyone sounded the same.

lines.narrate: Orin is turning the lid of the tea-tin over in his hands.

lines.text: Orin. You worked the Iron Road. You told me once, at Ashford, years ago. Escort work.
One season. Salt carts, over the pass and down to the coast. Commandery money. Good pay.
And Saltwick? Roke said Saltwick, and you went—
I know what I did.

lines.narrate: He puts the lid back on the tin, carefully, and presses it down all the way round.

lines.text: Not tonight.

choices.label: “Then not tonight. When you're ready.”

lines.text: Thank you.

lines.narrate: Nessa opens her mouth, and Maren puts a hand on her knee, and she shuts it again.

lines.text: He'd better, though. Eventually.
He will. He always does, in the end. It's the end that takes the time.

choices.label: “Orin. What happened at Saltwick?”

lines.text: We left. That's the whole of it. It isn't the whole of it, and I'm not telling the rest by a forge with that letter on the anvil.
That's not fair, you can't just say "we left" and—
Nessa.

lines.narrate: Orin gets up and goes out into the yard to check on Roke's horse, which does not need checking.

choices.label: Ask Maren what became of the keeper at Upper Morrow

lines.text: Sister Corra. She went for service when I was nineteen. The receipt said "released to duty". I asked what duty, and the officer said the Commandery's, and gave me more tea.
I never found out. I don't suppose he'd know. I don't suppose anyone wrote it down.
Someone always writes it down. That's what the Commandery is.
Then I'd like to read it.

rite-camp.location: The wall walk at Highpass, before dawn

wall.title: Under the Roots
wall.objective: Sit with Aster Vey and Maren on the wall.

lines.narrate: Before dawn you take the hand-bell up to the wall walk, because Aster Vey asked to hear the wind. Maren comes up after you with a blanket, and sits down on the other side of the little bell, and does not say why.

lines.text: Do you want to know what it was like? Nobody has asked. I think they think it would be rude.
I want to know if you want to tell it.

It was under the roots. That's how I think of it. The bell was in the vault, and the vault is under the Briarwood, and I could feel the roots growing. Very slowly. The way you would feel a clock, if you were inside it.
I knew I was something. I didn't know what. The name went first. Then the town. Then whether I had ever been a person at all, or had always been a bell that dreamed it had a sister.
The last thing to go was the third hour, rung flat. I kept that longest. I didn't know whose it was. I just knew it was wrong, and that I liked it wrong.
And tonight? With him?
That's what I wanted to tell someone. I thought I would be angry. I sat on his books and listened to him say my sister's name, and I wasn't angry. I was tired.
I want to know if that is a kind of forgiving, or a kind of giving up.

choices.label: “Neither. It's yours. It doesn't have to be a kind of anything.”

lines.narrate: The bell is quiet. Down in the lower camp, someone is starting a fire for the morning.

lines.text: I like that. Nobody has let me have anything that wasn't a kind of something for a long time.
Then have it.

choices.label: “It's giving up. Don't. Stay angry.”

lines.text: Perhaps. I'll try, if you think I should.
She doesn't owe him her anger. She doesn't owe us it, either.

lines.narrate: Maren tucks the blanket round the little bell, which cannot feel it, and leaves her hand there.

choices.label: Ask Maren what she thinks

lines.text: I think a man told you the truth tonight, about yourself, for the first time. That is tiring. It's meant to be.
Ask yourself again when you've slept.
I don't sleep.
Then ask me again when I have.

children.title: Biscuit and the Children from Cask
children.objective: Sit with Nessa and the children, then decide who goes to Vell.

lines.narrate: In the mess at Highpass sixty children are asleep on the floor in rows, under soldiers' cloaks. Three of them are not asleep. They are sitting by the hearth with Nessa and Biscuit.
In the barracks at Highpass the children from the pass are asleep in the bunks, two and three to a bunk. Three of them are not asleep. They are sitting by the stove with Nessa and Biscuit.

At the first night's camp on the road east to Fenmere, the children from the pass are asleep in the carts Fenmere sent. Three of them are not asleep. They are sitting by the fire with Nessa and Biscuit.

lines.text: ...and then he ate the whole thing. The whole pie, off the baker's sill. And the baker came out and said, whose dog is this? And Biscuit looked at me, and I looked at Biscuit, and I said, I've never seen this dog in my life.

lines.narrate: A girl of about seven, from Cask, considers this with great seriousness.

lines.text: Is that true?
Most of it.

lines.narrate: Biscuit has his chin on the smallest boy's foot, and the boy has stopped shivering.

lines.text: Do you have a stone where you live?
We have a bell. It's old. It rings every hour, and a boy called Pim rings it too, a breath after, and he's never once been late.
Our stone stopped.
I know. I know it did.

lines.narrate: Later, when the three of them are asleep against the dog, Orin sits down on Nessa's other side with two cups.

lines.text: Vell, then. Who goes.

lines.narrate: The council's answer has come by its own rider: the council asks the hero of the free wards to go to Vell for it, with its letter in your pack, and to come back.

lines.text: That's the council's answer. You swore to it. It's a good answer.

lines.narrate: A letter has come up from Briarwatch by the morning rider, in Tovin's hand. Briarwatch says go, and come home. Tovin says to keep the hand-bell by you. Pim has written something underneath, crossed it out, and written "good luck" instead.

lines.text: You swore to them. They've said.
You swore to us. So we're the ones who say. I say we go. All of us.
Obviously.
You swore to no one. So it's your call, nobody else's. I'll tell you what I think, if you want it. I think you've already decided.

lines.narrate: Word has come by the council's rider: the council would like the hero of the free wards to go to Vell, and to come back.

lines.text: I'm going. Whatever anyone says. Someone who isn't him has to see those nurseries.

choices.label: “We go together. All of us.”

lines.text: Good.
I'll pack the rope.

lines.narrate: Nessa looks down at the children asleep against Biscuit, and doesn't move, so as not to wake them, until the fire is nearly out.

choices.label: “We go. But we take the road slowly, and see what's on it.”

lines.text: Good. Corvane wants us there quickly. That's reason enough to be slow.
That's not a reason. That's a mood.
It's served me well.

lamp.title: Who Sits with Orin
lamp.objective: Decide who sits with Orin tonight.

lines.narrate: The first night on the Iron Road to Vell, Saltwick camps along a mile of the road in a long line of small fires, each family round its own. At the far end of the line, the last fire, Orin sits by himself with the salt-hall lamp, which he has cleaned and filled and not lit.

On Saltwick's roofs, the night after the tide, every lamp is lit. The town sits out on the slates to look at them. At the very edge of the town, on the cooper's yard roof where the planks run out, Orin sits by himself with the salt-hall lamp, which he has cleaned and filled and not lit.

Bram Tolley and Ella Marsh have gone with the convoy to Vell. Davin is sitting on the salt-hall roof in the place where his grandmother usually sits, because tonight Mags is sitting somewhere else, on her own.
Maren has a pot on your fire. She has been watching Orin's back for an hour.

lines.text: Someone should go and sit with him. I don't think it should be nobody. I'm not sure it should be me.

choices.label: Go and sit with Orin yourself
“You go, Maren. You've known him longest.”
“Leave him be tonight. He'll come to the fire when he wants to.”

lines.text: Perhaps. He's been leaving himself be for eight years. I'm not sure it's working.

lines.narrate: Orin does not come to the fire. Late in the night you see that he has lit the lamp after all, and is sitting with it, holding it up a little, at nothing.
You sit down on the other side of the lamp. He moves it, an inch, so that it is between you exactly.

lines.text: She said she'll think about it.

I've had eight years to think what she'd say. I had it all. She'd spit, or she'd forgive me, or she'd push me off the ladder. I'd got ready for all three. I hadn't got ready for her to think about it.
It's fair. It's the fairest thing anyone's ever done to me.

lines.narrate: That is all he says. After a while he picks up the lamp and turns it in his hands, and you understand that he has said as much as he can tonight, and that it is more than he has said to anyone before.

lines.text: Varn's still alive. Captain Odell Varn. Last I heard he had a company on the coast road, guarding grain. Good pay. He'd do the same again tomorrow and sleep after. He told me once that's what a captain is: someone who can.

I went to the guild at Ashford the next winter and asked to be posted where nobody would ask me to walk away from anyone. They laughed. Then they sent me to the bridge. Then I met Maren, and then I met you.

Last night I was at the back with the lantern, and everyone came up the road. Everyone. I counted twice in my head and then Maren counted out loud and I couldn't hear her for a bit because of my own heart.

Last night I was at the back with the lantern, and everyone came up the road. Some of them grey to the shoulder. But everyone. I counted them twice in my head and couldn't hear myself for a bit because of my own heart.

Last night I was at the back with the lantern, and everyone came up the road. Some of them grey to the shoulder. But everyone. I counted them twice in my head and couldn't hear myself for a bit because of my own heart.
I'd like to come back here one day. When it's over. Whatever it is. Not to be forgiven. To be some use to her for a season, and let her decide what that's worth.

choices.label: “Then we'll come back. When it's over.”

lines.text: We. All right. We.

lines.narrate: He lights the lamp, finally, from the fire, and sets it on the ground between you, and the two of you sit with it until Maren comes over with three bowls of something and sits down too.

choices.label: “You carried them out tonight, Orin. That counts for something.”

lines.text: It counts for tonight. Tonight isn't the one she's thinking about.

lines.narrate: But he lets you sit there, and after a while he lights the lamp.

Maren takes two bowls from the pot and goes along the road to the last fire. You can see them from where you sit, though you cannot hear them for a long time. She sits down beside him. She gives him a bowl. He looks at it.

lines.text: Is this the stew.
It's soup. It's entirely different.

lines.narrate: He eats it. All of it. Then, as the fire burns down, he talks, and Maren listens, and once she puts her hand on his arm and leaves it there.
He eats it. Then he says something short, and Maren nods, and they sit with the unlit lamp between them until the fire is low, not saying anything else.
Later, when she comes back, she sits down by you and does not say what he told her.

lines.text: He asked me to tell you he's all right. He isn't, and he knows I'll tell you that too. That's the closest he comes to lying, Orin: asking someone else to do it for him.

choices.label: “Thank you for going.”

lines.text: He'd have done it for me. He has done it for me. Twice. Neither time did I eat the soup.

vell-ysolde.location: The sluices under Vell's east wall, that night

sluice.title: The Sluices
sluice.objective: Ysolde Carr has been offered a way out of Vell.

lines.narrate: Nessa wakes you an hour before dawn with a hand over your mouth and Biscuit wet to the shoulders beside her.

lines.text: Don't say anything. Come on. Bring a lamp. Don't light it.

lines.narrate: Under Vell's east wall the river comes in through an iron grating and goes out again through the sluices, and Nessa has found the one place where the grating has rusted through. A flat-bottomed boat is tied up under it, stolen from somewhere, with two sacks in it, and a boy's coat with a button newly sewn on.
Ysolde Carr is standing on the sluice ledge, in her shawl, with her arms folded, looking at the boat.

lines.text: Jory and Wil are at the end of the sluice with Orin's rope. We take the boat down to the Iron Road ford and we're over the pass in four days. Briarwatch takes people. Briarwatch takes everybody. They'd be fed. You'd be — you'd be you. Get in the boat, Ysolde.
I came down here because you asked me to, and you've been kind to the boys, and I wanted to see it. I've seen it. It's a good boat.
No.
You don't get to say no to living, that's not — someone's made you think this is the only door, and it isn't, I'm standing in another one, look—

I know it isn't the only door. You've shown me. I'm grateful. I still don't want to go through it. Over the pass, the boys are two more mouths at the back of somebody else's line, in somebody else's town, for the rest of their lives. Here they're fed because of me. Here I'm a bell over the Sixth District, and every night I'll hear them breathing.
It's mine. It's the only thing I've ever had that's mine. Please don't take it off me because you're frightened for me.

lines.narrate: Nessa turns round and looks at you. Her face is wet. She is not going to say please; she never does. She is going to do whatever you say, and you can see that she knows it, and hates it.
There is a knock at your door an hour before dawn, very soft, and when you open it Ysolde Carr is standing in the corridor in her shawl with her arms folded.

lines.text: Sorry. I couldn't sleep. There's a place under the east wall where the sluice grating's rusted through. My brothers found it. They want me to go out through it tonight, and take them over the pass, and they've stolen a boat to do it. I went down and looked at it. It's a good boat.
I'm not going. I wanted to tell someone from the free wards that. So somebody over there knows I could have, and didn't. It's mine. It's the only thing I've ever had that's mine.

lines.narrate: She asks you to help her take the boat back to where the boys stole it from, before anyone notices, so that Jory and Wil are not in trouble for it. You do. On the way back she tells you about the Sixth District, every street of it, as if she were learning it by heart.

choices.label: Back Nessa: “Get in the boat, Ysolde. We'll take you all.”

lines.narrate: You step down onto the ledge beside Nessa, and say it too. The boys. The pass. Briarwatch. You say it as well as you have ever said anything.
Ysolde listens to all of it. Then she unfolds her arms and walks back up the sluice stair, past both of you, without hurrying, the way she walked up to the casting wall the first morning.

lines.text: Tell the boys to bring the boat back. They'll get in trouble. I'm going to bed.
We tried. At least we tried. At least nobody can say we stood there and let her—

lines.narrate: She doesn't finish. She sits down on the wet ledge with Biscuit and puts her face in his neck, and you sit down beside her.

choices.label: Back Ysolde: “It's her choice, Nessa. Let her make it.”

lines.text: Her choice. Her choice. Someone put her in a corner and painted a door on the wall and you're calling that—
Fine. Fine. It's her choice.

lines.narrate: She unties the boat herself, with fast angry hands, and pushes it off down the sluice towards where Jory and Wil are waiting, empty, and doesn't watch it go.

lines.text: Thank you. Both of you. Nessa, you as well. Especially you.
Don't. Don't thank me. I didn't do anything. That's the whole—

lines.narrate: Ysolde takes Nessa's hand anyway, and holds it, and after a moment Nessa lets her.

choices.label: Walk back up to the yard before the drill-guard wake

vell-camp.location: The guest-house off the drill-yard, the next evening

evening.title: Something New
evening.objective: An evening in Vell, seven days from the casting.

lines.narrate: The guest-house Fennick has assigned you (form nine, "accommodation, visiting, distinguished") has one fire and four chairs and a window onto the drill-yard. Maren has pulled her chair round so she does not have to look at the casting wall.
Nessa is not in her chair. She is out on the barracks steps with Biscuit, a little way from Ysolde, not talking to her.
Nessa is not in her chair. She is out on the barracks steps with Biscuit and Ysolde and the two boys, teaching Wil to whistle.

This morning Hesk's drill-guard asked the free wards' hero for a practice bout in the yard, in front of the barracks, by way of saying nothing at all about the night at the vault. You gave them one. It is Orin who brings it up, the way he notices a strap that has been re-buckled.

lines.text: This morning in the bout you took a pike-butt on the shield that should have put you on the flags. You didn't move. I've stood in shield walls twenty years and I felt that one land from across the yard.
Shield Wall, the old guild books call it. When you stop being a person holding a shield and start being a wall that happens to breathe.
You've changed your feet. In the bout you were inside the pikeman's reach before he'd finished deciding to thrust. That's not drill. That's something else.
You've been practising in the yard at dawn. I hear you. The same three steps, over and over, until they stop being steps.
In the bout, when they put four on you, you said 'hold' and I held. I wasn't even in it. I was on the step. I didn't decide to. I was holding before I'd heard myself agree.
Commanding presence, the guild books call it. I'd call it the thing that makes eight people stop being eight people.
In the bout they lost you. Eight of Hesk's best, in a bare yard, at noon, and they lost you. I couldn't see where you'd gone and I was watching.
You don't need the light any more, either. You crossed the barracks roof last week without a lamp. I'm not sure I like it. I'm very glad of it.
In the bout you had the sergeant's pike-strap cut before the first pass. He didn't notice till the head fell off. Hesk noticed.
You look at the corners of a room first now. I watched you walk into Fennick's office and check the hinges before the man.
You talked Fennick into giving us the room with the fire. Fennick. I watched him say no three times and then fill in form nine.
And I couldn't hear a single lie in it. You didn't tell him one. You told him the truth in the order he wanted to hear it. That's new. That's worse.
In the bout, when you cast, the flags cracked. All the way across. Oswin Pike has been out there with a broom all afternoon, swearing.
It hits harder. Everything you throw. Not wilder. Harder. As if you've learned to put more of yourself behind it and less of it to waste.

In the bout you moved before the pike did. You were out of its way before it was in yours. I've seen that once before, in an old sergeant who'd been in so many fights he'd stopped being surprised by them.
Foresight, the books say. A breath ahead of the moment. I wonder what it costs you to live a breath ahead of everybody.
Your circle, in the bout. The drill-guard couldn't get out of it. I watched a man walk into a line of chalk as if it were a wall, and stand there looking puzzled.
You've learned to draw a place and make it hold. In Vell. Of all the cities to learn that in.
A drill-guard boy went over on his ankle in the bout this morning. You put your hand on it, and he walked off the yard. He was back on the pikes by noon, telling everyone.
That was very good work. Better than mine. Don't look like that; it's allowed. Healer's grace. It comes to some of us late, and all at once.
In the bout, when you struck, the air rang. Like a bell. The drill-guard felt it in their teeth. The old ones put their pikes down and just listened.
Hallowed strikes. Every blow a small prayer, and the prayer lands. In a city that's forgotten what a ward sounds like.
In the bout you took a pike-butt under the arm and walked through it like rain. I looked for the bruise after. There isn't one.
Templar's mail. The faith holds where the iron doesn't. I've seen it twice in my life. Now three times.
The drill-guard's dogs. They were meant to be in the bout too. They wouldn't go for you. They went and lay down by Biscuit instead.
Beast bond, the wardens call it. Biscuit's been sleeping on your feet. He's never slept on anyone's feet but Nessa's.
The drill-guard's dogs. They were meant to be in the bout too. They wouldn't go for you. They sat down in a row in front of you, and waited to be told what to do.
Beast bond, the wardens call it. The cat in Fennick's office has started following you about the census hall. Fennick has not decided which form it goes on.
In the bout they set you a mark at the far end of the yard. You hit it, and then you hit the peg it hung on. I paced it after. Sixty paces.
Your breathing's changed when you draw. It goes very slow. I hear a lot of breathing. I've never heard anyone's go that slow and stay awake.
You took us over Saltwick's roofs in the dark and through Vell's back streets since and never once stopped to think which way. I've been here a week and I still get lost going to the well.
Wayfinding. You always know where the door is. It's a good thing to know, in this city.
You knew what the three locks on the iron vault were. Before anyone told you. You said the makers' names. Oswin Pike nearly dropped his lamp.
Deep lore. You've started knowing things the way I know a fever: before you've finished looking.
You sang in the bout. Under your breath. The drill-guard hit harder and the cuts closed, theirs as well as yours. They didn't know what to make of it. Neither did I.
Martial verse. The old war-singers had it. A song that fights and a song that mends, at once. You've found the part of a song that does both.
In the bout, they put eight pikes round you, and you talked to them as if you were at a council table. And they lowered them, and listened, as if they were.
A diplomat's poise. You don't raise your voice any more. You don't need to. People lean in.
You're different, these last days. Steadier. I can't say how. I'd know it in a fight, though. I knew it in the bout.
You've been learning something, on the road, all this year. You haven't said what. Whatever it is, it's started to show.

choices.label: “I had good teachers.”

lines.text: You had us. Not the same thing.
It's exactly the same thing, Orin. Say thank you.
...Thank you.

choices.label: “Seven days. I'd give it back for a way to stop the casting.”

lines.text: I know you would. That's why I'm glad it's you that has it.

lines.narrate: Out in the drill-yard, the furnace under the casting wall breathes up through the iron door, one day hotter. Nobody says anything else for a while.

witness-camp.location: The Iron Road, the first night out of Vell

road.title: The One She Could Not Hear
road.objective: Sit up with Maren on the road home.

lines.narrate: The first night out of Vell you camp at a dead echo-stone on the Iron Road, number sixty, with the pass a grey shape against the stars ahead of you. Everyone else is asleep. Maren is not. She is sitting with her back against the stone's post and Ysolde's button tin in her lap.

lines.text: Sixty-three. I gave him sixty-three. And Ysolde, and three hundred and thirty-six others, I said "true".
I burned it. Four hundred lines. Ysolde's was the last line in it. I wrote "true" beside her name before I burned it. I don't know why. I suppose so that it had been written down once.
A hundred and ninety stayed, when nobody made them. And I said "true" to every one, and I heard nothing under any of it. Ysolde first.

She was the one I couldn't hear. Not because there was nothing there. Because there was everything there, and all of it was true. She's thought about it every night since her mother died. She's made it true the way you make a path: by walking it until it's there.

And I sat across the table from her and said "true", and she smiled at me as if I'd given her something. I'd given her the only thing I had. It wasn't what she needed. I don't know what she needed. I don't think anyone in Vell has ever had it to give.

lines.narrate: She turns the button tin over. It rattles.

lines.text: I used to keep a list. You remember. Every keeper who'd been lost, and I couldn't rest until each one had an ending. I let it go, in Merrowgate harbour.
I find I want to start one again, with one name on it. And I'm frightened of what kind of list it would be.
I still have my list. You know I do. Every keeper who was lost, and one space on it I've never filled, because I was waiting for the right word.
I find I want to write her name in the space. Before anything has happened to her. And I'm frightened of what kind of list that would make it.

choices.label: “Then keep one name. Not a list. Just her.”

lines.text: Just her.

lines.narrate: She takes a stub of pencil out of her sleeve, and writes it on the inside of the button tin's lid, small: Ysolde Carr, Sixth District. Then she closes the lid.

lines.text: Not an ending. A name. I'll try to tell the difference.

choices.label: “You told the truth. That's all anyone could ask of you.”

lines.text: That's what everyone will say. That's what I'd say, to someone else.
It isn't all anyone could ask. It's all anyone did ask. I'd like, once, for someone to have asked me for something harder.

choices.label: Say nothing, and sit with her

lines.narrate: You sit down against the other side of the post. After a while she leans her head back against the iron, and closes her eyes, and does not sleep, and neither do you. Towards dawn she reaches round the post and finds your hand, and holds it, and lets go.

tower.title: The First Bell She Chose
tower.objective: Aster Vey has something to ask.

lines.narrate: That night Pim comes to the forge to find you, without his coat, and says that Aster is asking for you. Only you. Before anyone else. Tovin is sitting at the foot of the tower stair with the rope across his knees, and he does not come up.
At the top of the stair the great bell is warm under your hand.

lines.text: You asked me first, in the spring. Before you answered Corvane. You came up here and asked what I wanted. Nobody had ever done that. So I'm asking you first. As a friend. Before I ask anyone who votes.

lines.narrate: It is Aster Vey who asks the council, at the end of the session, after the vote. Tovin carries the hand-bell into the reeve's hall and sets it on the long table in front of Aveline, and sits down at the back, and does not look at anyone. You hear it with everyone else.

lines.text: Vell had a great bell once, before Central Command melted it for the stones. Corvane is going to cast it again. He means to put four hundred people in it.

I want to go. Not now. If it comes to it. If Vell needs its heart held, and the only way is someone in the bronze, I want it to be me. I know what it is. I'm the only one of all of them who does. Every one of those four hundred will say yes to a door. I'd be saying yes to a room I've lived in.

If I go, Briarwatch's bell is empty. You need to know that before you answer. The Gloam will come to the edge of the Briarwood every winter. The village will have to keep a watch. Tovin knows. Tovin's known for a week.
You can't. You live here. Tovin, tell her she lives here.
I told you on the stair, Pim. She was made to live here. This would be the first bell she ever chose.

lines.narrate: Tovin's hands are shaking on the rope. His voice is not.
Tovin's hands are shaking in his lap. His voice is not.

Tomorrow she will put it to the wards' seat on the council, and you already know what will happen there, because the wards have talked about nothing else for a week: they will split, half and half, Cinder Fold's hearth bells for and Fenmere's little bells against. It will come back to you. It was always going to.

The wards' seat votes on it, there and then: the hand-bells and hearth bells of every town that sent one. They split, half and half, Cinder Fold's for and Fenmere's against, and Aveline looks down the table at you, because there is nobody else left to ask.
The wards have no seat on the council to put it to. It is yours to answer, here, tonight.
The wards have no seat on the council to ask. Aveline says that it is not the council's to say, then, and looks down the long table at you, because it was you who carried her to Vell and back.

lines.text: So. Tell me. May I go, if it comes to it? Or do you want me to stay?

choices.label: “If it comes to it, you may go. It's yours to choose.”

lines.text: Thank you. You don't know what that is, to be told it's mine.

lines.narrate: Pim goes out without a word, very fast, and across the square. Tovin does not go after him. He sits very still, with his hands together.

lines.text: He'll be back. He always is. He'll want to know the hours for Vell, so he can ring them here, and I'll have to look them up for him.
Ring them gently.

choices.label: “Stay. Briarwatch needs its bell, and I need you here.”

lines.narrate: The bell is quiet for a long time.

lines.text: All right. I'll stay. You asked, and I'll stay. I want you to know that I wanted to go. I want somebody to know that.
You're staying? You're staying.
Pim. Let her be sad about it. She's allowed. She'll come with you to Vell all the same, to see it, and then she'll come home.

lines.narrate: Pim sits down beside Tovin, close, and does not say anything else.

home-camp.location: The square at Briarwatch, the last evening before Vell

hours.title: The Hours
hours.objective: The last evening at home before going back over the pass.

lines.narrate: At dusk on the last evening Tovin rings the hours. Everybody in the square stops to hear it: the farmers loading their carts, the river-meadow people coming up the mill lane with their baskets, Aveline on the reeve's hall step with a letter in her hand. Nobody says anything until he has finished. Then for a little while nobody says anything after that, either.
Inside the bell, Aster Vey rings with him. It sounds, tonight, like somebody saying goodbye to a room before a journey.
Inside the bell, Aster Vey rings with him, exactly on the hour, the way she has every evening since the bell came back.

Later, by the well, there is a boy from the river meadow sitting on the step with Brannagh's goat. He is about eight, from Cask, and he has it on its rope, and is feeding it the ends of a cabbage one leaf at a time, very seriously. Brannagh is on the bench by the forge, watching him. She does not get up.

lines.text: She's let him have the goat. She doesn't let anyone have the goat. She brought it to the Vote. She brought it to a council of war.

lines.narrate: Biscuit goes over and sits down beside the boy and the goat, the way he does with anyone small who is being serious about something. The boy puts a hand on his head without looking at him.

lines.text: Biscuit says he's a good minder. Biscuit says the goat thinks so too. Don't look at me like that, Biscuit's got opinions, he's allowed.
There's nobody left in my lower village to mind her. Nobody's minded her for two years but me. He asked. Nobody else ever asked.

I'm going to write to Ysolde. About the goat. I'm going to tell her there's a boy from Cask minding a goat in Briarwatch and nobody's making him do it. I don't know why. I think I want her to know there are places where that happens.

choices.label: “Write it. Send it this time.”

lines.text: This time. Yes. All right. I always say that. This time I mean it.

lines.narrate: She writes it on her knee by the well, by the last of the light, and seals it with candle-wax from the forge, and gives it to the Vell courier herself before she can change her mind.

choices.label: Sit on the step with the boy and the goat for a while

lines.narrate: You sit down on the well step. The boy moves up to make room, and goes on feeding the goat. Nessa sits down on your other side with Biscuit. Nobody says anything for a long time, and it is the easiest silence you have had since the spring.

lines.text: I'll write it tomorrow. Tomorrow. Probably.

vault-camp.location: The drill-yard at Vell, at dawn, above the vault

lines.narrate: Nobody goes to bed. You sit on the iron rim of the vault door at dawn, with the stair going down into the dark below your boots, and the drill-yard empty, and the river wall grey in the first light.
Down in the vault the bells are cold. When you put your ear to the stair you hear nothing at all.
Down in the vault the floor is bare, where the bells stood. Out along the river wall, very faint, you can hear iron bells ringing out of time.
Nobody makes a joke. Nobody tries. After a long time, somebody says one thing they will remember, and then everybody does, one each, round the rim of the door.

lines.text: The plates. A number and a date on every one of them, riveted on. Somebody stood there with a hammer thirty-one times. I'll remember that somebody did that, and went home for supper.
And the two who said no. They kept saying it, the whole time he was reading. I'll remember that I heard them and I let it happen.
The girl from Lindmoor. Hanne. Fourteen. She carried the keeper's water. She asked Aster to hold her hand, and Aster said she was. I'll remember that Aster said she was.
One of the ones who didn't answer, when Aster asked. I don't know her name. She's on the river wall now. I'll remember that I don't know what she wanted.
The one who was singing. The evening hymn, flat, over and over, all the time we were down there. I've got it in my head and I'm not going to let it go. Somebody should have it.
The boy at the end. Number Thirty-One, from Osgood's Cross. He asked me whether he'd done something wrong. I said no. I said he'd been in the wrong room. He said that was what they told him, too.

lines.narrate: Then it is your turn.

choices.label: “The register. The same word on every page: 'present'.”

lines.narrate: You say it. People taken for standing in a room. Nobody answers. The sun comes up over the river wall, and Oswin Pike comes across the yard with the tin box under his good arm, and sits down on the rim of the door with you, and does not open it.

choices.label: “Corvane, in front of the last bell, with nothing to say.”

lines.narrate: You say it. Across the drill-yard, Corvane is on the wall walk above the casting wall, with his ledger, where he reads the lost at dusk. He is not reading. He is standing there with it closed, looking at the river.

choices.label: Say nothing, and listen to the morning

lines.narrate: You do not say anything. Nobody asks you to. The drill-yard fills slowly with ordinary sounds: a cart, a dog, a woman calling a child in for breakfast. Somebody in the volunteers' barracks is singing the evening hymn at the wrong end of the day, flat, very quietly.

b3-partone-end.location: Highpass, then Dera's forge at Briarwatch

corvane.title: The Keeper of the Names
corvane.objective: Decide what becomes of High Warden Corvane.

lines.narrate: Highpass, the morning after, at the top of the pass. Hesk is in a cell two doors down from Sable's, and has asked for nothing but a pencil. Corvane is in the guardroom with Captain Sorrel, sitting very straight on a hard chair, with his ledger on his knees.

lines.text: Him I can hold. He broke no law of ours till he walked over the pass with three hundred pikes. This one I don't know what to do with. He's cast fifty living people into bronze. He did it in the open, and they asked, and the council never made a law against it, because nobody imagined we'd need one.

lines.narrate: Iona, beside her, says that the council has had a grim summer since the vote, and will not be gentle with anyone from Vell, and that she would like that recorded before anyone decides anything.

lines.text: You brought him. You decide, and I'll write it down.
I've no objection to being decided about. I've decided about a great many people. I'd like to keep the ledger, if it's allowed. If it isn't, I'd like someone to promise to read it.

choices.label: Send him to the council's judgement

lines.narrate: You tell Sorrel: the council should judge him. In the open, in Aveline's hall, with the doors open so the square can hear, the way he did everything.

lines.text: Thank you. That's fair. I'd like a table, and a lamp to read by, if they're going to take a while. They usually do.

lines.narrate: Sorrel gives him the cell across from Sable's, because it has the best light. Sable, through the bars, asks him whether he is comfortable, and Corvane says that he is not, and Sable says good.

choices.label: Leave him to his own people

lines.narrate: You tell Sorrel: he is Vell's, not the free wards'. Let Vell's people decide what he is owed.

His own people are in the camps below Highpass and on the road down to the free wards, eighteen thousand of them, with nowhere to go. He goes down the mountain to them that afternoon with Roke beside him and the ledger under his arm, to be wherever they are.
He goes back down the Iron Road to Vell that afternoon with Roke beside him and the ledger under his arm, to stand in the drill-yard and let his city decide what he is.

lines.text: They might hang me. They might not. Either way it will be theirs. That's what I wanted for them. I find I want it for myself as well.

choices.label: Let him keep the ledger, as keeper of the names

lines.narrate: You tell Sorrel: let him keep the ledger. Somebody has to read the names. Nobody else ever has.
He will keep Fennick's box as well, and the names of a city that is now a list. Fennick has said that he can have it on one condition: that he reads the first page aloud, every night, first.

He will go back to Vell and stand on the wall walk at dusk and read the lost, as he has every night for a year, and the cast as well, now, every one of them, by name. And the first page. He says he will read the first page aloud from now on.

lines.text: Keeper of the names. That's a better title than High Warden. I'd have liked to have it first.

forge.title: Dera's Forge
forge.objective: Home, at the end of the summer.

lines.narrate: Briarwatch, at the end of the summer. You walk into the forge and Dera has your gear on the bench before you have finished saying hello. All of it. She has been waiting with the fire up since somebody saw you on the Briarwood road.

lines.text: Sit down. Don't talk yet. Let me look at it first and then you can tell me how you did it, and I'll tell you whether you were lying.

lines.narrate: She turns your gear over on the bench, piece by piece, the way she has since the bell, reading it like a letter.

lines.text: You stood in a doorway at Vell, they tell me, and eight people behind you came out of it alive. Bulwark Stand, the old guild books call that. Every one of them behind your shield at once. This buckle's taken the weight of it. I'll put a new one on.
There's a nick on the flat of your blade where you took somebody's sword out of his hand at the last echo-stone. Disarming Flourish, that is. My father could do it. Hold still, I'll dress the edge.

Roke says three hundred men put their pikes down at stone one, and that when you said "now" at the end, all your people moved at once. Coordinated Assault, the drill-books call it. I call it a miracle, with pikes.
Somebody marked a man for you at the echo-stone, they say, and he never saw where it came from. Death Mark. I don't want to know. I'll sharpen it. I don't want to know.
There's soot in every seam of this coat. Smoke and Snares, is it, now? Half a column of drill-guard coughing in a field and their pikes tied in knots. Iona will want to know who pays for the pikes.

Roke says you turned one of Hesk's own sergeants round at the echo-stone with three sentences and he fought his own side for a minute before he noticed. Turncoat Gambit. I've known merchants who'd sell their mothers for that.
Your staff's scorched at the tip in a fork. Like lightning. Chain Lightning, they say, and it went down a whole line of pikes at once. Don't point it at my anvil.
They say you reached back a heartbeat at the echo-stone and gave Maren's breath back to her before she'd lost it. Stolen Second. I've no idea what that does to a clock. I'd keep away from mine.
Pim says you called a guardian up out of the ground at Vell, and it stood over all of you like a wall. Summon Guardian. He's told the whole village. He's drawn it on the tower stair in chalk.

There's a shine on your hands that doesn't wash off. Shield of Faith, the shrine-sisters call it: everyone near you standing a little straighter and harder to hurt. They say it like it's a thing you'd want to be careful with.
Somebody at stone one said you judged a man without lifting a hand, and he went white and dropped his blade. Judgment. I've had customers I'd have liked to try that on.
They say you called down a crusade at the last echo-stone, and everyone on your side healed and went forward at once. Crusade. It's a big word for a forge. I'll just mend the mail.
Every dog in the lane has followed you up from the square, and there were wolves on the Iron Road that went through Hesk's camp like a flood when you called. Stampede. Keep them out of my hens.
There's an arrow-mark on stone one, Roke says, dead in the middle of the plate, from a hundred paces in the dark. Heartseeker. I've fletched you a dozen new ones. Don't waste them on posts.
You led three hundred men round the Hollins bend into open ground, they tell me, and they never knew where they were till the arrows landed. Ambush Ground. I'd have liked to see Hesk's face.
They say you said a word at the echo-stone and a man forgot what he was about to do. Word of Unmaking. Don't say it in here. I've got enough I've forgotten.
Roke says you sang at stone one and every one of your people went in together, braver than they meant to be. War Anthem. Sing it at the harvest. Nobody here can keep a tune.
They say you stood between two lines of pikes at the echo-stone and made them a bargain, and both sides took it. Grand Bargain. Aveline wants you on the council. I said you'd run.
You've learned something new on that road. I can see it in how you carry yourself, the way I can see a weld. I don't know what it is. Neither do you yet, I think.
Now. Gossip. All of it. That's the price. It always was.
Mags said she'd think about it. She hasn't sent word. I'm not going to Saltwick till she does. It isn't mine to decide when she's finished thinking.
I'm writing to Ysolde. Again. I've written her four. I sent two. I'm going to send this one. It's about the goat.
I'm writing about Ysolde. Not to her. About her. To nobody. I'm going to send it anyway. I'm going to send it to Wil. He can keep it for when he's older.
I've kept no list. I've kept her button tin. That's all. That's enough.

lines.narrate: Up in the tower, on the hour, the Briarwatch bell rings. It is Tovin ringing it, by hand, on the rope, because there is nobody in it now to ring it with him. A breath after him, Pim rings the hand-bell on the tower step. He has learned Vell's hours from the old bell-books, and he rings those too, after ours, very gently.

Up in the tower, on the hour, the Briarwatch bell rings. Tovin rings it, and Pim rings the hand-bell on the tower step a breath after, and inside the bronze Aster Vey rings with both of them, exactly on time.
Dera puts down her hammer to listen, as she always does. Then she picks it up again.

choices.label: Open the letter that came up with the Highpass post

letter.title: A Letter from Vell
letter.objective: A letter, from over the pass.

lines.narrate: There is a letter with the Highpass post, sealed in grey wax, in a neat clerk's hand you know. It has come over the pass in four days, which is fast.

"To the one who broke the Single Voice, at Briarwatch. From Clerk-Major Fennick, at what was Vell. I have come back into the city with two clerks to finish the census of what was left behind. It is irregular. Nobody else was going to."
"To the one who broke the Single Voice, at Briarwatch. From the records office at Vell, by the hand of the High Warden's clerks, the High Warden being held at Highpass."
"To the one who broke the Single Voice, at Briarwatch. From the records office at Vell, by the hand of the High Warden's clerks."
"To the one who broke the Single Voice, at Briarwatch. From the records office at Vell, by the hand of the clerks of the Keeper of the Names."

"I report, for the record, that the iron vault under the drill-yard was found open on the morning of the fourteenth. The three keys are on Sergeant Pike's belt, where they should be. The vault was opened with them nonetheless, by someone who knew where the sergeant sleeps."

"The round door at the far end of the vault is open. It was not forced. It was unlocked. Beneath it there is a stair. It is not iron and it is not Commandery work. It is cut in the rock, very old, and it goes down further than our lamps."
"There are chalk marks on the first steps, and the prints of three pairs of boots, going down. None coming up. Someone has opened the iron door under the vault, and gone down."
"I have entered it in the log as 'persons unknown, descending'. I do not know what else to call it. I thought you would want to know."
To be continued.

choices.label: Fold the letter, and put it in your coat
